 El Niño puts public agencies on high alert 
 Drain clearing. equipment checks are part of preparations for a stormy season 
 By TO Acorn Staff 
 on 
 October 30, 2026 
 By Michael Montalvo 
 mmontalvo@theacorn.com 
 RAIN AHEAD— Weather forecasters are predicting a particularly bad El Niño season, and public agencies have started to prepare for it. Acorn file photo 
 This week’s few sprinkles may be just a taste of what’s to come, as weather experts warn that a powerful El Niño could bring a much wetter season in the months ahead. Local government agencies aren’t waiting to see if the predictions come true before acting.
 Thousand Oaks has been preparing for this rainy season earlier than in any previous year.
 El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which sea surface temperatures become warmer than average in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. The pattern is often associated with heavy rainfall, flooding and storms.
 However, forecasters say this year is different: This El Niño is classified as a historic “super” El Niño, meaning there is an 83% chance it will become the strongest on record, according to the National Weather Service.
 Long-term ocean warming, rising global tropical ocean temperatures and climate change have supercharged this storm cycle, the experts say.
 Local government agencies said they began preparing 30 to 45 days earlier this year in anticipation of potentially severe rainstorms and to ensure residents have access to necessary supplies.
 “The city’s preparation process is ongoing and designed to reduce the risk of localized flooding, protect critical infrastructure, support the continuity of essential services, and ensure crews can respond quickly if significant storms occur,” said Alexandra South, city spokesperson.
 The work includes everything from cleaning and preparing storm drains to practicing access to and use of the Ventura County Emergency Operations Center notification systems and procuring additional sandbags and gravel bags, South said.
 She added that residents can also help by keeping leaves and debris out of gutters and drains near their homes, avoiding flooded roadways and following city communications for storm preparedness information and updates on sandbag distribution. 
 At the Sept. 3 Conejo Recreation and Park District board meeting, Andrew Mooney, director of parks and planning, said preparations were still underway.
 “We’ve already been clearing drains,” Mooney said. “Doing a lot of work out in the open space, making sure things are safe and ready to go so when we do have some storms, we’re prepared and ready to take that on as it comes.”
 Patrick Belavic, park superintendent for the CRPD, told the Acorn that the district had already conducted tree inspections and thinning, created a list and schedule of employees willing to respond to emergencies after normal work hours, kept fuel trucks topped off, and tested generators to ensure they were fueled and ready to go.
 “I think the city does a good job throughout the year keeping large drains clear, which in turn allows for our drains to perform better,” he said. “As long as we are communicating and staying on top of areas we know get hit hard, we will be fine.”
 County agencies and departments are also coordinating efforts to reduce potential impacts, strengthen emergency readiness and help residents prepare for severe weather.
 This week, the Acorn observed county staff clearing storm channels along farmland outside Camarillo. In addition to inspecting and maintaining critical infrastructure, the county’s Public Works Agency is monitoring roads and other areas that may be vulnerable to flooding or storm damage.
 Heavy rainfall can increase the risk of flooding, landslides and debris flows, particularly in areas previously affected by wildfires and other locations vulnerable to storm-related hazards. Strong El Niño conditions can also increase the risk of high surf in coastal areas that do not typically experience such conditions, particularly when storms coincide with peak high tides. However, this risk would not directly affect Thousand Oaks.
 The Ventura County Fire Department is also preparing personnel and resources for potential storm response while providing residents with information on flood preparedness and steps they can take to protect themselves, their families and their property.
 The county has issued a warning and is encouraging residents to take steps now to prepare for possible impacts. County officials urge residents to prepare their homes, learn their evacuation routes and sign up for VC Alert.
 “While we cannot predict exactly what this winter will bring, we know that early preparation can make a significant difference when severe weather occurs,” said Patrick Maynard, director of emergency services. “Our focus is on preparing early, coordinating closely with our cities and partner agencies, and making sure residents understand the hazards that may affect their communities.”
